As organizations prepare for 2027, workforce planning is becoming about more than filling open positions. Businesses are rethinking how they attract talent, develop teams, and build the flexibility needed for long-term success.

Here are four trends worth watching:

1. Skills-Based Hiring
Employers are placing greater emphasis on demonstrated capabilities and transferable skills, looking beyond traditional qualifications to identify strong candidates.

2. AI and Workforce Evolution
As AI becomes more integrated into business operations, organizations will need professionals who can adapt, embrace new technologies, and apply critical thinking.

3. Flexible Workforce Strategies
Temporary, contract, and permanent hiring solutions will continue to play an important role in helping businesses respond to changing demands.

4. Strategic Leadership Planning

Last week, Cognizant CFO Jatin Dalal told investors that AI agents could eventually handle 30 to 40 percent of the company’s client work. He added that if Cognizant only grows 15 percent over the next five years, its workforce would shrink.

That is a CFO telling Wall Street that his own headcount is a variable, not a constant.

He is not the only one saying it. TCS cut 23,000 employees in FY26, its largest single-year reduction ever. Its chairman talked about deploying half a million AI agents.

Across the top five Indian IT firms, combined headcount fell by nearly 7,000 in FY26. Bench strength dropped to under 12 percent in three years. It is expected to hit 8 to 10 percent by FY27.

The business model is what is actually shifting. Dalal described 2026 as one of the most competitive pricing years in three years. Cognizant is moving away from billing by the number of people deployed and toward outcome-based contracts where clients pay for results.

When AI agents handle the predictable 30 percent of delivery and the client pays for outcomes instead of bodies; the math changes everywhere. For revenue. For margins. For hiring.

The question is not whether AI replaces 30 - 40 percent of the work. That part is already in motion. 

The question is whether these companies can grow fast enough to absorb the people that the agents are displacing and whether the service companies can nudge thier customers to outcome-based contracts vs buying IT services by the hour.

A man explained to me today that my profession is no longer needed. And now I'm wondering whether it's time to shut down the business.

Here's what happened.

On Friday, a guy messages me. He found me himself, has been reading my posts, likes our B2B lead generation case studies. Wants to know how we work. Specifically, whether we get paid for results.

I explain. Nicely, in detail. What we do, what we're responsible for, how our pricing works. We charge a monthly retainer, not a commission on closed deals.

Today he replies.
Not interested. Salespeople, he says, get paid for results. And AI can already build contact lists and do outreach, so there's no point hiring humans for that anymore.
Well. That gave me something to think about.

We have a client in the US construction industry for whom we generate more than ten B2B leads every month. We have an investment project where we've been arranging three conversations with potential investors a month. Our clients are happy. They keep working with us.

And apparently, all they had to do was ask ChatGPT.

But the AI part isn't even what fascinates me most.
It's the sincere belief that a service provider should only get paid when a sale closes.
So let's say we find a potential buyer, understand their needs, get them interested, and arrange a meeting. Then our client's sales director spends six months negotiating. Or forgets to follow up. Or discovers that their product costs 40% more than the competition.

And somehow, that means we've been working for free for six months.
The sales director, meanwhile, still gets a salary. Funny how that works.
I do understand why clients like this arrangement. I'd probably enjoy it too if all my contractors were willing to finance my business risks out of their own pockets.
But I think there's something else going on here.

People are increasingly confusing having access to a tool with no longer needing professional expertise.

AI writes code. Why hire developers?
AI drafts contracts. Why pay lawyers?
AI finds contacts. Why bother with business development specialists?
My suspicion is that AI isn't making good professionals less valuable. It's making it harder to charge premium prices for basic mechanical tasks.
Which, by the way, is a very good thing.

And I suspect my correspondent and I live in two entirely different economic universes.
So now I'm curious.

Would you agree to get paid only for results if half the factors determining those results were completely outside your control?

Or am I missing something, and it's really time to quit and become a prompt engineer?
Do tell. I'm genuinely curious.

AI Doesn't Just Need Intelligence. It Needs Context.
Imagine hiring a brilliant employee with exceptional knowledge and problem-solving skills.
Now ask them to make an important business decision without explaining the customer, business rules, or previous decisions.
Would you expect the right decision every time?
Probably not.
The same principle applies to AI.
As we move from Generative AI that answers questions to Agentic AI that can reason, plan, and take actions, an important discipline comes into focus:
Context Engineering.
It's about designing what information an AI system receives at each step so it can understand the situation and respond effectively.
And it goes far beyond writing better prompts.
Consider a simple business example.
A customer asks an AI agent:
"Why is my invoice higher this month?"
Without sufficient context, the AI may provide a generic explanation.
With the right context, it can examine the customer's contract, pricing rules, usage history, discounts, and billing adjustments to explain the actual difference.
The AI model hasn't changed. What changed is the context available to it.
But here's an important distinction:
More context doesn't always mean better context.
The challenge is providing the right information, at the right time, without overwhelming the AI with irrelevant or outdated data.
My perspective:
Prompt Engineering helps us communicate with AI.
Context Engineering helps us design the information environment in which AI operates.
As AI moves toward executing complex business workflows, this distinction becomes increasingly important.
Are we investing enough in engineering the context surrounding AI intelligence?

AI-specialist job postings grew 69% in 2025, but the skills companies need are still evolving quickly.

Anthropic just reported a $104 billion loss. It's also days away from what could be the biggest IPO ever.

Both are true. Only one of them should worry you.

From its filing, nine months to Sep 30, 2026:

Revenue: $33.2B, up roughly 1,200% year on year.

Net loss: $104B.

But $94.3B of that loss is a non-cash charge from re-valuing convertible notes and similar deals. The business itself lost about $1.3B.

So the scary headline is mostly a side effect of the company getting more valuable. Accounting, not burn.

The number I'd actually watch is a different one: commitments.

Anthropic lists $900.9B in compute and infrastructure commitments, against about $132B in cash and short-term investments.

That's a bet that revenue keeps compounding. Run-rate hit $81B at the end of October, up $10B in a month. Brilliant, as long as it doesn't stall.

The market seems to believe it. Orders are reportedly about 6x the shares on offer, at $70-78 a share, with Nasdaq trading as ANT expected around Nov 19.

Founder lesson at any size: read three lines, not one.

Operating loss tells you if the business works. Cash tells you how long you have. Commitments tell you what you've promised before you've earned it.

Small companies get hurt on that third line too. Long leases, fixed vendor contracts, hiring ahead of revenue.

If you could buy ANT at the IPO price, would you? And which line of the filing decides it for you?

- being very raw and not afraid of hurting someone's feelings (professionally) 
- stay away from anything that AI throws your way (using AI for ideas and research is OK, just stay away from the content itself) 

That takes less than several hours a week if you know what you're doing.

Using AI on a bid is allowed. Answers nobody checked are what lose the marks.
7 signs an evaluator spots, and the fix for each.

UK guidance for public buyers says bidders can use AI, much like hiring a bid writer. It also tells buyers to verify accuracy rather than assume it. So the claims in your answers are more likely to be tested at clarification or presentation.

The answers that get caught tend to look alike. They answer a nearby question, carry no names or numbers, and open the same way as the answer before. An evaluator reading six of them in a row notices quickly.

What fixes it is a short check before anything goes in:

1. Answer the question that was asked
→ Use its wording and answer its parts in order

2. Put one real example in each answer
→ Client, year and result

3. Back every claim with evidence you could show
→ If you couldn't show it at clarification, cut it

4. Open with the answer
→ Proof second, company background last

5. Make the risks specific to this contract
→ Name the risk and the person who owns it

6. Read it aloud
→ Cut the words your team wouldn't say in a meeting

7. Check promises against the price
→ Each commitment needs a line in the pricing schedule

Twenty minutes per answer is a lot less than losing a 20% question because the evaluator stopped trusting it.

Which of the seven do you see most often in reviews?
